title: Testosterone therapy in hypogonadal men: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
article_subtype: Systematic review with a network meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials and a narrative synthesis of non-randomised studies
condition_or_topic: Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) in hypogonadal men
clinical_background: Testosterone deficiency can adversely affect male sexual function and quality of life. Clinical guidelines recommend TRT for symptomatic adult men with low testosterone to relieve symptoms and raise testosterone into the mid-normal range for young men. Earlier meta-analyses suggested benefits for quality of life, depression and aspects of sexual function, but individual trials reported mixed findings. Evidence about cardiovascular and other harms was also conflicting: two large observational studies reported increased cardiovascular risk, prompting safety warnings, while other analyses did not find an increased risk. Because testosterone products and dosing strategies differ, treating all products as a single intervention may obscure differences between them.
objectives: Assess the relative benefits and harms of individual testosterone products in hypogonadal men.
clinical_question: In adult men with low testosterone, how do individual TRT products, compared with placebo, another TRT product or the same product at a different dose, affect quality of life, depression, libido, erectile function, activities of daily living, testosterone levels and reported adverse outcomes?
interpretation: When TRT products were analysed together, treatment improved quality of life, depression, libido and erectile function relative to placebo. Comparisons of individual products showed few differences: none improved depression or erectile function significantly relative to placebo in the network meta-analysis, and oral TU (160mg/day) performed worse for libido than most other treatments. The analyses did not identify a statistically significant increase in major adverse events, but the authors caution that rare harms cannot be assessed adequately given the studies’ risk of bias and generally short treatment and follow-up periods.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The benefits observed for TRT as a class and the absence of a detected increase in individual cardiovascular events are consistent with most earlier meta-analyses. Earlier reviews of cardiovascular safety nevertheless reached conflicting conclusions; the authors note that a re-analysis using a random-effects model did not retain the significant increase reported by one review. Observational findings also conflict: Vigen and colleagues reported increased cardiovascular risk, whereas other large studies reported lower risks among TRT users. The authors consider Vigen and colleagues’ participants’ comorbidities and frequent patch use relevant to generalisability. They excluded Finkle and colleagues’ study because baseline testosterone was not reported and the cohort was not restricted to androgen deficiency, although they regard its finding about non-fatal MI during the first 90 days after prescription as concerning. The Testosterone Trials reported improved sexual outcomes after 1year with 1% testosterone gel, but were not powered to detect adverse events; the authors state that those findings should not be extended to other preparations.
clinical_implications: Although TRT showed benefits when treated as a class, major improvements were not observed with any individual product.
The absence of a statistically significant increase in major harms should be interpreted cautiously because serious events were rare and most studies had limited treatment and follow-up durations.
Findings for 1% testosterone gel in The Testosterone Trials should not be assumed to apply to other testosterone preparations.
limitations: Studies used different testosterone assays and different thresholds for defining low testosterone.
The included RCTs and NRS generally had unclear or high risk of bias, potentially affecting the reliability of subjective outcomes.
Treatment and follow-up may have been too brief to detect effects on all outcomes, including adverse events; the median treatment duration in RCTs was 6 months.
Poor reporting of harms and treatment groups in NRS prevented pooling their results by meta-analysis.
Information on men aged 65 years and older was insufficient for the planned analysis of individual products because most RCTs enrolled broad age ranges.
Low event rates prevented robust network estimates for cardiovascular death and restricted network analyses of other harms.
Network consistency could not be assessed for quality of life, depression or erectile function because the networks lacked closed loops.
Publication bias could not be excluded for most outcomes.
strengths: The authors searched published and grey literature comprehensively, without language or date restrictions.
Eligibility was restricted to studies enrolling men with total testosterone ≤12nmol/L or free testosterone ≤225pmol/L.
The review compared benefits and harms across individual testosterone products, including products without direct head-to-head trial comparisons.
open_questions: Why oral TU (120mg/day) appeared more effective for libido than oral TU (160mg/day) remains unresolved.
The longer-term risk of rare adverse events with TRT remains uncertain.
Evidence remains insufficient to compare individual testosterone products specifically in men aged 65 years and older.
future_directions: Investigate the unexpected libido findings for the different oral TU doses.
Conduct longer-term, high-quality studies to assess rare harms more fully.
Design and conduct future studies rigorously, with comprehensive reporting of methods to support appraisal and interpretation.
study_design: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 87 RCTs and 51 NRS. The review was registered prospectively as CRD42014009963. Searches of MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL and grey literature were updated on 25 May 2017. RCT findings were pooled; NRS findings were summarized narratively.

population.description: Adult men with low testosterone levels. Across the included RCTs, study-level mean participant ages ranged from 30 years to 78 years.
inclusion_criteria: Studies enrolling men aged ≥18years with total testosterone ≤12nmol/L or free testosterone ≤225pmol/L.
Placebo-controlled or active-controlled RCTs and NRS evaluating a testosterone product for at least 12 weeks.
Cross-over trials whose initial treatment period lasted at least 12 weeks.
exclusion_criteria: Studies that artificially suppressed endogenous testosterone.
Studies with a treatment duration shorter than 12 weeks.

interventions: Any form of testosterone replacement therapy (TRT); in the network analyses, each dose of an individual product was treated separately.
comparators: The same TRT at a different dose
statistical_methods: The article did not designate outcomes as primary or secondary. Outcomes of interest were quality of life, depression, libido, erectile function, activities of daily living and total testosterone level at 3 months, 6 months and the end of the study; harms outcomes were cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, prostate cancer, diabetes, heart disease, serious adverse events, withdrawals due to adverse events and erythrocytosis. RCT data were analysed by pairwise meta-analysis and Bayesian network meta-analysis, while NRS data were summarized narratively. Analyses used change from baseline for quality of life, depression, erectile function and libido, and post-treatment values for total testosterone. Network analyses used binomial likelihood for dichotomous outcomes and normal likelihood for continuous outcomes, included multiarm trials and applied a continuity correction for zero-event harms. Results were reported from random-effects models as MD, SMD or OR, as appropriate, with 95% CrIs or CIs. Model fit and inconsistency were assessed where possible; exploratory analyses removed trials enrolling men with major comorbidities. Publication bias was assessed by visual inspection of funnel plots.
follow_up: RCT treatment duration had a median of 6 months (range: 3–36 months). The study characteristics describe NRS durations of up to 8 years; a separately described prospective cohort followed men for up to 10 years.
quality_assessment_tool: Cochrane Collaboration’s risk of bias tool for RCTs; SIGN50 for cohort studies.

main_findings.description: When testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) products were analysed together, quality of life improved significantly compared with placebo.
main_findings.context: Pairwise meta-analysis of 23 RCTs assessing quality of life; n=2834 in the placebo comparison; I2=71%. The analysis used a random-effects model.

main_findings.description: IM TU at 1000mg/12 weeks significantly improved quality of life compared with placebo.
main_findings.context: Network meta-analysis; the reported interval is a 95% credible interval. The quality-of-life network comprised 23 RCTs and 14 treatments in addition to placebo.

main_findings.description: IM TU at 1000mg/12 weeks significantly improved quality of life compared with oral TU at 160mg/day.
main_findings.context: Network meta-analysis; the reported interval is a 95% credible interval. No other between-treatment differences in quality of life were significant.

main_findings.description: TRT products considered together improved depression compared with placebo.
main_findings.context: Pairwise meta-analysis; n=786; I2=44%. Depression was assessed in 12 RCTs involving 852 participants allocated to nine treatments. The analysis used a random-effects model. The network meta-analysis found no significant depression difference for any individual TRT versus placebo or between treatments.

main_findings.description: TRT products considered together significantly improved libido compared with placebo.
main_findings.context: Pairwise meta-analysis; n=2732; I2=74%. Libido was investigated in 14 RCTs involving 3167 patients allocated to 10 treatments. The analysis used a random-effects model.

main_findings.description: Most individual treatments significantly improved libido relative to placebo.
main_findings.context: Network meta-analysis. Gel 1% at 100mg/day performed significantly better than patch at 5mg/day and oral TU at 160mg/day; oral TU at 120mg/day performed significantly better than patch at 5mg/day and gel 1% at 75mg/day. Oral TU at 160mg/day performed significantly worse than 8/9 other TRTs in the network.

main_findings.description: TRT products considered together improved erectile function compared with placebo.
main_findings.context: Pairwise meta-analysis; I2=74%. Erectile function was assessed in 17 placebo-controlled RCTs involving 3165 patients allocated to nine treatments. The analysis used a random-effects model. In the network meta-analysis, no individual TRT differed significantly from placebo or another treatment.

safety_results.discontinuations: For withdrawal due to adverse events, 48 RCTs reported placebo: 150/2551 and TRT: 221/2840 over 12 weeks to 36 months. The random-effects comparison was not statistically significant, although withdrawals tended to be more frequent with TRT: OR 1.31 (95%CI 0.98 to 1.73); I2=13%. In the network analysis, testosterone patch at 5mg/day was associated with higher odds of withdrawal than placebo and many other TRTs.
notable_adverse_events: Cardiovascular death: across 18 RCTs lasting 12 weeks to 36 months, placebo: 4/1851; TRT: 9/2088. The random-effects comparison found no significant difference: OR 2.15 (95%CI 0.72 to 6.45); I2=11%. The low event rate prevented robust network estimates.
Myocardial infarction: across 15 RCTs lasting 12 weeks to 36 months, placebo: 10/1613; TRT: 6/1915. There was no significant increase with TRT: random-effects OR 0.43 (95%CI 0.15 to 1.19); I2=34%.
Prostate cancer: across 13 RCTs lasting 12 weeks to 36 months, placebo: 11/1649; TRT: 12/1877. There was no significant increase with TRT: random-effects OR 0.97 (95%CI 0.43 to 2.23); I2=0%.
Stroke: across 8 RCTs lasting 12 weeks to 36 months, placebo: 8/1103; TRT: 8/1104. There was no significant increase with TRT: random-effects OR 0.99 (95%CI 0.37 to 2.65); I2=29%.
Heart disease: across 3 RCTs lasting 40 weeks to 12 months, placebo: 5/120; TRT: 5/131. There was no significant increase with TRT: random-effects OR 0.89 (95%CI 0.24 to 3.26); I2=0%.
Erythrocytosis: across 4 RCTs lasting 12 weeks to 12 months, placebo: 0/78; TRT: 4/110. There was no significant increase with TRT: random-effects OR 2.44 (95%CI 0.26 to 22.53); I2=0%.

Serious adverse events: across 18 RCTs lasting 12 weeks to 36 months, placebo: 181/1902; TRT: 168/2138. The random-effects comparison found no significant increase: OR 0.88 (95%CI 0.70 to 1.11); I2=0%. The network analysis found no significant difference between any TRT and placebo or between TRTs.
Incident diabetes: no RCT reported this outcome during treatment.

subgroup_analyses: After RCTs enrolling men with major comorbidities were excluded, the pooled quality-of-life benefit versus placebo changed to SMD –0.17 (95%CI –0.34 to –0.01), with I2=62%, compared with I2=71% in the full analysis. The network result remained consistent despite the removal of three treatments.

After trials enrolling men with major comorbidities were excluded, the pooled depression comparison was no longer statistically significant: SMD –0.12 (95%CI –0.49 to 0.26); I2=56%. The network findings did not change after two treatments were removed.

After trials enrolling men with major comorbidities were excluded, the pooled libido comparison was no longer statistically significant: SMD 0.19 (95%CI –0.03 to 0.41); I2=80%. Network results remained consistent for the treatments retained after four treatments were removed.

After trials enrolling men with major comorbidities were excluded, the pooled erectile-function estimate was SMD 0.36 (95%CI 0.21 to 0.51); I2=58%. Network findings did not change after two treatments were removed.
secondary_results: The review identified 87 RCTs and 51 NRS published between 1997 and 2017; 70 RCTs and 19 NRS reported an outcome of interest. RCT treatment duration had a median of 6 months (range: 3–36 months), and mean participant age across RCTs ranged from 30 years to 78 years. Among the NRS, 10 were retrospective cohorts and 9 were prospective cohorts.
One RCT in men with mild cognitive impairment found no significant difference in activities of daily living between testosterone gel at 50–100mg/day and placebo after 6 months (p=0.31).

For total testosterone levels, 26 RCTs reported measurements after 3 months, 23 after 6 months, and 57 at the end of treatment. Levels were significantly higher than with placebo for 6/15 treatments at 3 months and 11/18 at 6 months. By the end of treatment, spanning 12 weeks to 36 months, 26/28 testosterone therapies were associated with levels above 12nmol/L, and 17 of 28 treatments produced significantly higher levels than placebo.

Comparison of the network consistency and inconsistency models found no evidence of inconsistency for libido or total testosterone levels. Consistency could not be assessed for quality of life, depression or erectile function because those networks lacked closed loops.

Harms reporting in the NRS was generally inadequate. In the longest prospective cohort, which included 656 men followed for up to 10 years, recipients of IM TU at 1000mg/12 weeks had a lower incidence of death than men receiving no TRT: TRT group 0.0092 (95% CI 0.0032 to 0.0368); no TRT group 0.1145 (95% CI 0.0746 to 0.1756). Cardiovascular causes accounted for 0 of 2 deaths in the TRT group and 19 of 21 in the control group. Non-fatal events were TRT group: 0 MI and 0 stroke; no TRT group: 26 MI and 30 stroke.

In a retrospective cohort including 8808 men dispensed TRT and 35527 men never dispensed TRT, the TRT group had lower risks over a median follow-up of 3.4 years: sudden cardiovascular death, aHR 0.76 (95%CI 0.61 to 0.93); acute MI, aHR 0.74 (95%CI 0.63 to 0.86); and stroke, aHR 0.64 (95%CI 0.52 to 0.80).

In contrast, an earlier retrospective cohort of 8709 men who had undergone angiography reported a higher risk of an adverse cardiovascular event among those who filled a TRT prescription than among those without one: aHR 1.29 (95%CI 1.05 to 1.58). The discussion gives a different lower confidence limit for this cited study: 95%CI 1.04 to 1.58.

A retrospective cohort comparing injection and gel TRT users with low baseline testosterone found no significant difference in MI (aHR 1.64, 95%CI 0.57 to 4.69), stroke (aHR 1.28, 95% CI 0.27 to 6.02) or death (aHR 5.53, 95%CI 0.98 to 31.15).

Prostate cancer was reported by 10 NRS. A prospective registry of 999 newly diagnosed hypogonadal men found no statistically significant difference between TRT users and non-users: incidence rate ratio 0.52 (95%CI 0.22 to 1.26).

In the prospective cohort reported by Traish and colleagues, prostate cancer occurred in 7/360 men given TRT as IM TU and 12/296 men given no TRT over a median follow-up of 7 years. In the prospective study by Yassin and colleagues, prostate cancer biopsies were positive in 16.7% of TRT users versus 51.9% of non-users, with lower staging and grading severity among users. A small retrospective cohort of men previously diagnosed with prostate cancer reported no recurrences among TRT users during 36 months of follow-up.

tables.title: Indirect comparisons of testosterone products for quality of life
tables.summary: The table presents random-effects estimates based on changes from baseline; a negative standardised mean difference denotes better quality of life. The article identifies a significant improvement with IM TU, 1000 mg/12 weeks, relative to placebo and to Oral TU, 160 mg/day. The remaining cells are left empty because their placement within the treatment-comparison matrix cannot be established reliably from the document.

tables.title: Adverse-event meta-analysis comparing testosterone treatment with placebo
tables.summary: These random-effects comparisons found no statistically significant increase in the listed adverse outcomes with TRT as a class versus placebo. Withdrawals due to adverse events were more frequent in direction, but the difference was not statistically significant. No RCT reported incident diabetes during treatment.

main_conclusion: Considered together, testosterone products improved quality of life, depression, erectile function and libido compared with placebo, but comparisons of individual products found few differences. The authors found no increased risk of major harms in the available evidence, while cautioning that study bias, uncommon serious events and generally short treatment and follow-up limit safety conclusions.
narrative_summary: This systematic review and network meta-analysis examined the relative benefits and harms of testosterone products in adult men with low testosterone. It included 87 RCTs and 51 non-randomised studies; 70 RCTs and 19 non-randomised studies reported an outcome of interest. Randomised evidence was pooled for comparisons of TRT as a class with placebo and for comparisons among individual products. As a class, TRT improved quality of life (SMD –0.26, 95%CI –0.41 to –0.11), depression (SMD –0.23, 95%CI –0.44 to –0.01), libido (SMD 0.33, 95%CI 0.16 to 0.50) and erectile function (SMD 0.25, 95%CI 0.10 to 0.41). In the treatment network, IM TU (1000mg/12 weeks) improved quality of life relative to placebo; most individual treatments improved libido, but none showed a significant benefit over placebo for depression or erectile function. Randomised comparisons did not establish increased odds of cardiovascular death or other major adverse events with TRT as a class. Withdrawals due to adverse events tended to be higher with TRT than with placebo (OR 1.31, 95%CI 0.98 to 1.73), without statistical significance; patch (5mg/day) was associated with increased withdrawal odds in the network comparison. Most included studies had high or unclear risk of bias and relatively brief treatment and follow-up. The authors therefore call for longer, rigorous studies to assess uncommon harms more fully.

document_sections.heading: AbstrAct
document_sections.content: This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared individual testosterone products in hypogonadal men. Searches of MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL and grey literature were updated on 25 May 2017. Eligible randomised-controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomised studies (NRS) treated men for ≥3 months and compared testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) with placebo, another TRT or a different dose of the same product. Outcomes covered quality of life, depression, libido, erectile function, activities of daily living, testosterone levels and specified cardiovascular, prostate, metabolic and other harms. RCT findings were synthesised by meta-analysis and network meta-analysis. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane’s risk of bias tool for RCTs and Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN)50 for NRS. The review included 87 RCTs and 51 NRS; most had high or unclear risk of bias and brief treatment and follow-up. Against placebo, TRT considered as a class improved quality of life (standardised mean difference (SMD) −0.26, 95% CI −0.41 to –0.11), libido (SMD 0.33, 95%CI 0.16 to 0.50), depression (SMD −0.23, 95%CI −0.44 to –0.01) and erectile function (SMD 0.25, 95%CI 0.10 to 0.41). Individual products improved libido more often than the other outcomes (6/10 products versus placebo). Only one individual product improved quality of life versus placebo; none improved depression or erectile function in the network comparisons. No statistically significant overall increase in adverse events was observed, although some TRTs increased withdrawals because of adverse events. The authors found a class-level improvement in those symptoms without major improvements attributable to individual products. They considered longer-term, high-quality trials necessary to assess harms adequately. The review was registered as CRD42014009963.

document_sections.heading: strengths and limitations of this study
document_sections.content: The review searched published and grey literature extensively for randomised and non-randomised studies of adult men with low testosterone. Because there is no universally accepted diagnostic threshold, eligibility required total testosterone ≤12nmol/L or free testosterone ≤225 pmol/L, in line with recent guidelines. Harms reporting in NRS was too poor for meta-analysis. Included studies generally had high or unclear risk of bias, and treatment and follow-up were usually relatively brief. Longer, high-quality studies are needed to assess uncommon adverse events more fully.

document_sections.heading: IntrODuctIOn
document_sections.content: Testosterone deficiency adversely affects male sexuality and quality of life. Recent clinical guidance recommends TRT for symptomatic adult men with low testosterone, aiming to raise levels into the mid-normal range for young men. Two large observational studies reported greater cardiovascular risk with testosterone use; the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Health Canada warned about a possible increase in cardiovascular events. Earlier meta-analyses reported benefits versus placebo for quality of life, depression and some aspects of sexual function, but individual trial results varied across formulations and doses. Harms meta-analyses also disagreed: a 2013 analysis found increased cardiovascular-related events in a population containing both hypogonadal and eugonadal men, whereas other analyses found no increase in outcomes including myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death. Because products and dosing approaches differ, combining every testosterone treatment into one category may be inappropriate. The authors therefore reviewed RCTs and NRS in hypogonadal men and compared individual products through network meta-analysis.

document_sections.heading: MEthODs
document_sections.content: The review was registered prospectively as CRD42014009963 and followed the Cochrane handbook and the PRISMA for Network Meta-Analysis checklist. It considered RCTs and NRS involving adult men with low testosterone who received any TRT, with placebo, a different TRT or another dose of the same TRT as comparator. Studies were not excluded because of which outcomes they reported.

document_sections.heading: Patient involvement
document_sections.content: Patients did not set the research question or help plan the study design or implementation. A patient representative helped choose outcomes, and patient groups could comment on the protocol. Patients were not asked to interpret or write the results. The authors did not plan to distribute the findings to study participants or the relevant patient community.

document_sections.heading: search strategy
document_sections.content: On 3 June 2014, searches covered Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid MEDLINE In-Process & Other Non-Indexed Citations, Embase Classic+Embase and CENTRAL in the Cochrane Library; grey literature was searched using CADTH’s Grey Matters Light. Every search was updated on 25 May 2017. Controlled terms included ‘Testosterone’, ‘Testosterone Congeners’, ‘Androgens’ and ‘Hormone Replacement Therapy’, with relevant terms for dosing, derivatives, adverse events and therapeutic use. Keyword searches combined testosterone or androgen terms with administration routes or treatment-related terms; they also covered ‘TRT’ and product names including AndroGel, Bio-T-Gel and Striant. Search syntax was adapted to each database. The full strategy was provided in supplementary eAppendix 1.

document_sections.heading: study selection
document_sections.content: Eligible placebo-controlled or active-controlled RCTs and NRS enrolled men aged ≥18years with total testosterone ≤12nmol/L or free testosterone ≤225pmol/L and administered a testosterone product. Studies were excluded if they artificially suppressed endogenous testosterone, used testosterone precursors or enrolled fewer than 10 participants. Treatment had to last at least 12 weeks, a generally recommended follow-up point; a cross-over trial qualified only when its initial period lasted at least 12 weeks. Titles and abstracts underwent duplicate screening, potentially eligible full texts were evaluated, and disagreements were settled by consensus.

document_sections.heading: Data extraction and risk of bias
document_sections.content: One reviewer extracted data with piloted standardised Distiller SR forms, and another checked the extraction. Only initial-period results were taken from cross-over trials. Two reviewers assessed RCT risk of bias with the Cochrane Collaboration’s risk of bias tool and cohort-study risk of bias with SIGN50, resolving disagreements by discussion. Publication bias was examined visually with funnel plots.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes
document_sections.content: Continuous outcomes were quality of life, depression, libido, erectile function, activities of daily living and total testosterone at 3 months, 6 months and study end. Dichotomous outcomes were cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, prostate cancer, diabetes, heart disease, serious adverse events, withdrawal because of adverse events and erythrocytosis. Quality-of-life, depression, erectile-function and libido results were accepted only when measured on validated scales; scale directions were standardised before analysis. Higher effect estimates signified improvement in libido, erectile function and testosterone, whereas lower estimates signified improvement in quality of life and depression. RCT data informed benefits and testosterone levels; both RCTs and NRS informed harms.

document_sections.heading: Data analysis
document_sections.content: NRS results were described narratively rather than pooled. RCT data underwent meta-analysis in RevMan (V.5.3; Cochrane Collaboration) and Bayesian network meta-analysis in WinBUGS (V.1.4.3; MRC Biostatistics Unit). Quality of life, depression, erectile function and libido were analysed as mean changes from baseline; total testosterone was analysed using mean post-treatment values. Benefit and testosterone analyses used the number randomised as denominator, while harms analyses used the number treated. Two trials were excluded from analyses because their outcome data were outliers with a substantial effect on heterogeneity. An exploratory analysis removed trials enrolling men with major comorbidities: HIV/AIDS, osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, angina, Alzheimer’s disease, heart failure or end-stage renal disease. Network analyses included every trial reporting the relevant outcome, irrespective of comorbidity, and treated each product dose as a separate network node. Dichotomous and continuous outcomes used binomial and normal likelihood models, respectively; the approach accommodated multiarm trials. A continuity correction addressed zero-event harms. Model fit and the fixed-versus-random-effects choice were evaluated through the deviance information criterion and residual deviance relative to unconstrained data points; reported estimates came from random-effects models. Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimation supplied point estimates and 95% credible intervals (CrIs); effects were presented as appropriate using MD, SMDs with SDs, or ORs with 95% CrIs or CIs. Basic parameters received vague priors, for example N(0, 1002). Convergence checks used trace plots and Brooks-Gelman-Rubin statistics. Each analysis fitted three chains with at least 20000 iterations and at least 20000 burn-in iterations. Where possible, consistency and inconsistency models were compared using deviance, between-study variance and deviance information criterion, with posterior mean deviance plotted for individual data points. NodeXL was used to construct network diagrams.

document_sections.heading: role of the funding source
document_sections.content: The funder did not participate in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Every author could access the complete study data, and the corresponding author made the final submission decision.

document_sections.heading: rEsults search results and study characteristics
document_sections.content: The search identified 87 RCTs and 51 NRS published from 1997 to 2017, represented by 196 records. Outcomes of interest were reported by 70 RCTs and 19 NRS. RCT treatment lasted a median of 6 months (range: 3–36 months), and mean participant ages ranged from 30 years to 78 years. Most RCTs compared against placebo (87%) and had two treatment groups (89%). The NRS comprised 10 retrospective and 9 prospective cohorts, with study duration up to 8 years. Few studies had low risk of bias, principally because randomisation, allocation concealment or analysis populations were insufficiently described. Visual funnel-plot assessment could not exclude publication bias for most outcomes. The PRISMA figure depicts study selection; another figure presents the quality-of-life meta-analysis.

document_sections.heading: network consistency
document_sections.content: Comparisons between consistency and inconsistency models found no evidence of inconsistency for libido or total testosterone. Consistency could not be assessed for quality of life, depression or erectile function because their networks lacked closed loops. Supplementary material provides network characteristics and evidence diagrams.

document_sections.heading: Outcomes Quality of life
document_sections.content: Quality of life was assessed in 23 RCTs involving 3090 participants: 21 were placebo-controlled and two active-controlled. Pooling TRT products against placebo showed significant improvement (SMD –0.26, 95%CI –0.41 to –0.11; n=2834), with substantial heterogeneity (I2=71%). Removing RCTs enrolling men with major comorbidities changed heterogeneity little (I2=62%) and yielded SMD –0.17, 95%CI –0.34 to –0.01. The network included 23 RCTs and 14 treatments besides placebo. IM testosterone undecanoate (TU; 1000mg/12 weeks) improved quality of life significantly versus placebo (SMD −0.48, 95%CI −0.84 to –0.10) and versus oral TU (160mg/day; SMD −0.68, 95%CI −1.32 to –0.02). Other treatment comparisons were not significant. Excluding major-comorbidity studies removed three treatments without changing the qualitative result. A figure depicts the network, with node size indicating randomised sample size and connecting lines indicating the number of direct-comparison RCTs. Table 1 presents indirect product comparisons as standardised mean differences with credible intervals.

document_sections.heading: Depression
document_sections.content: Depression was examined in 12 RCTs involving 852 participants assigned to nine treatments; 11 trials were placebo-controlled and 1 active-controlled. Pooling products showed improvement versus placebo (SMD –0.23, 95%CI –0.44 to –0.01; n=786; I2=44%). Excluding trials of men with major comorbidities did not reduce heterogeneity and made the pooled effect statistically non-significant (SMD –0.12, 95%CI –0.49 to 0.26; I2=56%). In the network, neither individual TRTs versus placebo nor comparisons between active treatments showed significant depression differences. Removing major-comorbidity trials eliminated two treatments but did not change this finding.

document_sections.heading: Libido
document_sections.content: Libido was investigated in 14 RCTs involving 3167 patients and 10 treatments; 12 trials were placebo-controlled and 2 active-controlled. Pooled TRT significantly improved libido versus placebo (SMD 0.33, 95%CI 0.16 to 0.50; I2=74%; n=2732). Removing studies of men with major comorbidities increased heterogeneity (I2=80%) and left a statistically non-significant estimate (SMD 0.19, 95%CI –0.03 to 0.41). In network comparisons, 6/10 individual treatments improved libido significantly versus placebo. Among active treatments, 1% gel (100mg/day) outperformed patch (5mg/day) and oral TU (160mg/day); oral TU (120mg/day) outperformed patch (5mg/day) and 1% gel (75mg/day). Oral TU (160mg/ day) performed significantly worse than 8/9 other TRTs in its network. Excluding major-comorbidity trials removed four treatments, while findings for the remaining treatments stayed consistent.

document_sections.heading: Erectile function
document_sections.content: Erectile function was evaluated by 17 placebo-controlled RCTs involving 3165 patients assigned to nine treatments. Pooled TRT improved erectile function compared with placebo (SMD 0.25, 95%CI 0.10 to 0.41), with substantial heterogeneity (I2=74%). After trials of men with major comorbidities were removed, heterogeneity fell to I2=58% without a qualitative change in the estimate (SMD 0.36, 95%CI 0.21 to 0.51). Network analysis found no significant differences between any individual TRT and placebo or between active treatments. Removing major-comorbidity trials eliminated two treatments but did not alter that result.

document_sections.heading: Activities of daily living
document_sections.content: One RCT in men with mild cognitive impairment found no significant difference in activities of daily living after 6 months of testosterone gel 50–100mg/ day versus placebo (p=0.31).

document_sections.heading: Testosterone levels
document_sections.content: Total testosterone after 3 months was reported in 26 RCTs and after 6 months in 23 RCTs; 57 RCTs reported end-of-treatment levels. Roughly half the treatments in the respective networks produced significantly higher levels than placebo at 3 months (6/15) and 6 months (11/18). At treatment end, spanning 12 weeks to 36 months, 26/28 testosterone therapies were associated with total testosterone above 12nmol/L, while 17 of 28 treatments produced significantly higher levels than placebo.

document_sections.heading: Cardiovascular death
document_sections.content: Ten RCTs reported cardiovascular deaths during treatment, and another nine reported that none occurred; the analysis included 18 placebo-controlled RCTs. Pairwise pooling of all TRT products found no statistically significant difference from placebo in cardiovascular-death risk (OR 2.15, 95%CI 0.72 to 6.45; I2=11%). Sparse events prevented robust network estimates, which were not reported. A figure displays the pooled comparison. Table 2 summarises adverse-event meta-analyses for TRT as a class versus placebo.

document_sections.heading: Other adverse events
document_sections.content: Pairwise meta-analysis found no increased odds versus placebo for myocardial infarction, stroke, prostate cancer, heart disease, erythrocytosis or serious adverse events with TRT considered as a class. Withdrawals because of adverse events tended to be more frequent with TRT, but the comparison was not statistically significant (OR 1.31, 95%CI 0.98 to 1.73; I2=13%). No RCT reported incident diabetes during treatment. Sparse events restricted network meta-analysis to serious adverse events and adverse-event withdrawals. Serious adverse events did not differ significantly between any TRT and placebo or among TRTs. Testosterone patch (5mg/day) was associated with greater odds of withdrawal because of adverse events than placebo and many other TRTs. Table 2 gives the event counts, treatment durations, pooled odds ratios and heterogeneity measures for the adverse-event outcomes.

document_sections.heading: non-randomised studies
document_sections.content: Harms reporting in NRS was generally inadequate: group sizes, event counts by group, and product type or dose were often unclear. In the longest prospective cohort, 656 men were followed for up to 10 years. Recipients of IM TU (1000mg/12 weeks) had a lower incidence of death than untreated men: TRT group 0.0092 (95% CI 0.0032 to 0.0368) versus no TRT group 0.1145 (95% CI 0.0746 to 0.1756). Cardiovascular causes accounted for 19 of 21 control-group deaths and 0 of 2 TRT-group deaths. Non-fatal events were also more frequent without treatment: TRT group 0 MI and 0 stroke versus no TRT group 26 MI and 30 stroke. A large USA retrospective cohort compared 8808 men dispensed TRT with 35527 never dispensed TRT. Over a median 3.4 years, the TRT group had lower risks of sudden cardiovascular death (adjusted HR (aHR) 0.76, 95%CI 0.61 to 0.93), acute MI (aHR 0.74, 95%CI 0.63 to 0.86) and stroke (aHR 0.64, 95%CI 0.52 to 0.80). Conversely, an earlier retrospective cohort of 8709 men who had undergone angiography associated filling a TRT prescription with greater cardiovascular-event risk than having no TRT prescription (aHR 1.29, 95%CI 1.05 to 1.58). Another retrospective cohort found no significant injection-versus-gel difference among users with low baseline testosterone for MI (aHR 1.64, 95%CI 0.57 to 4.69), stroke (aHR 1.28, 95% CI 0.27 to 6.02) or death (aHR 5.53, 95%CI 0.98 to 31.15). Prostate cancer was addressed by 10 NRS. A prospective registry of 999 newly diagnosed hypogonadal men found no statistically significant risk difference between TRT users and non-users (incidence rate ratio 0.52, 95%CI 0.22 to 1.26). A prospective cohort reported prostate cancer in 7/360 men given IM TU versus 12/296 untreated men during median follow-up of 7 years. Another prospective study reported positive prostate-cancer biopsies in 16.7% of TRT users versus 51.9% of non-users, with lower stage and grade among users. A small retrospective cohort of men with previously diagnosed prostate cancer reported no recurrence among TRT users over 36 months. Most remaining studies inadequately identified either the treatment assignment of men developing prostate cancer or treatment-group denominators.

document_sections.heading: DIscussIOn
document_sections.content: The authors note that TRT remains disputed despite more than 70 years of clinical use and suggest that differing actions of testosterone preparations may contribute. They combined pairwise and network meta-analysis to assess products, including indirect comparisons where no head-to-head trial existed. Their class-level findings—improvements in quality of life, depression, libido and erectile function without an observed increase in cardiovascular death or other major harms—agree with most earlier meta-analyses. Individual products did not differ significantly for depression or erectile function. For libido, testosterone gel (1%, 100mg/day) outperformed testosterone patch (5mg/ day) and oral TU (160mg/day); oral TU (160mg/ day) performed worse than most network treatments, including oral TU at 120mg/day. The greater apparent efficacy of the lower oral TU dose was unexpected and needs investigation. Evidence about cardiovascular harm remains conflicting. FDA and Health Canada issued alerts in 2015 partly on the basis of two observational studies. Vigen and colleagues studied men with low testosterone after angiography and reported greater risk for a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction and stroke (aHR 1.29, 95%CI 1.04 to 1.58). In that cohort, 63% used a patch, and substantial comorbidity could limit generalisability. Finkle and colleagues reported higher non-fatal MI risk during the first 90 days after a testosterone prescription; their retrospective cohort lacked baseline testosterone data and was not restricted to androgen deficiency, so it was ineligible for this review, although the finding remains concerning. Other recent large observational studies found lower cardiovascular-death, stroke and MI risks among TRT users; earlier observational studies reported lower all-cause mortality in hypogonadal TRT users. Previous meta-analyses also disagreed: one found increased cardiovascular adverse events, whereas several did not. The analysis by Xu and colleagues used a broad composite spanning cardiac and vascular conditions and was criticised for its fixed-effects model; a later random-effects re-analysis found no significant increase. The authors’ results align with prior meta-analyses finding no increased risk of individual cardiovascular events versus placebo. A planned analysis of individual products for men aged 65 years and older was limited because most RCTs enrolled broad age ranges. The Testosterone Trials addressed older men and, after 1year of 1% testosterone gel, reported better desire and erectile function among those with low baseline sexual function without an apparent cardiovascular-event increase. Those trials lacked power to detect adverse events, and their findings should not be extended to other preparations.

document_sections.heading: strengths and limitations
document_sections.content: Strengths included a broad search of published and grey literature without language or date restrictions and restriction to studies enrolling men with total testosterone ≤12nmol/L or free testosterone ≤225pmol/L. The authors acknowledge that no threshold for low testosterone is universally accepted; a recent guideline recommends TRT below total testosterone 12nmol/L. Limitations included variation in testosterone assays and low-testosterone cut-offs across studies, a problem also noted elsewhere. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s hormone standardisation project may help address it. RCTs and NRS generally had unclear or high risk of bias, potentially reducing confidence in subjective outcomes. Treatment and follow-up might have been too short to show effects on some symptoms or adverse events. Although eligibility required treatment for 3 months or longer, consistent with advice to reassess symptoms after 3 months of TRT, median RCT treatment lasted 6 months and some symptoms could take longer to resolve. Finally, some individual RCTs reported benefits for depression or erectile function against placebo, whereas no individual product showed such a benefit in the network meta-analysis. The authors note that this previously described phenomenon produces more conservative effect estimates.

document_sections.heading: cOnclusIOns
document_sections.content: The authors describe this as the first comparison, to their knowledge, of benefits and harms across individual testosterone products in hypogonadal men, including products rarely compared directly. TRT pooled as a class improved quality of life, depression, erectile function and libido versus placebo, but head-to-head product comparisons showed few differences. No increase in major harms was found; that finding requires caution because included studies had high risk of bias, serious harms were rare, and treatment and follow-up were usually short. The authors call for future studies with rigorous design and execution and sufficiently detailed methods to support appraisal and interpretation.
